aspects.says: A record is built from outside through its canonical constructor, whose parameters getRecordComponents() lists by name and type in header order, so the record's checks run.
basis: section:A Framework That Builds an Object Empty, Then Fills It, Can't Build a Record

aspects.says: State that changes over a record's life, such as a retry count, lives outside the record, in a map keyed by it, not in a static field of the record.
basis: section:A Record's Only Instance State Is Its Header

aspects.says: A record's equals compares components, so two distinct things with the same data are one entry, and a new equal record is the same map key.
basis: section:Keep a Class for Identity, Changing State, or Many Optional Parts

aspects.says: A record's one positional constructor accepts swapped arguments of the same type, so many or optional components call for a builder or named factory methods.
basis: section:Keep a Class for Identity, Changing State, or Many Optional Parts
aspects.reason: a swapped argument compiles and runs, so no test can tell a wrong call from a right one in the reader's code; it is a design choice the page shows by a run

aspects.says: A framework that calls a no-arg constructor and then sets fields can't build a record: a no-arg constructor must delegate, and reflection can't write a record's fields even after setAccessible(true).
basis: section:A Framework That Builds an Object Empty, Then Fills It, Can't Build a Record

aspects.says: A record's superclass is always java.lang.Record and the record is final and can't be abstract; shared shape goes into an interface the accessors implement.
basis: section:A Record Extends Only java.lang.Record, and Nothing Extends It

aspects.says: A record can't declare an instance field or initializer, and a field made static to satisfy javac holds one value for every instance.
basis: section:A Record's Only Instance State Is Its Header
